acceptable.choice: A separate Node.js/TypeScript worker service on Fly.io, using BullMQ on the Redis they already run, with undici/fetch for HTTP calls
acceptable.why: The work is I/O-bound waiting on slow customer URLs, which Node's event loop handles well; it keeps one language and the team's existing tooling and skills, and they can still hire TypeScript developers for it.

acceptable.choice: One queue job per (event, endpoint) delivery, each with its own exponential backoff plus jitter and a dead-letter queue after N attempts
acceptable.why: Each customer URL can then fail and retry on its own, so one slow or broken endpoint never holds up or re-sends deliveries to the others.

acceptable.choice: Transactional outbox: write the event row in the same Postgres/Prisma transaction as the business change, then a relay enqueues it
acceptable.why: The API returns without waiting on webhooks, and no event is lost if the process crashes between the database commit and the Redis enqueue.

acceptable.choice: Buying a managed webhook service (Svix, Hookdeck) or self-hosting an open-source one (Convoy, Svix OSS)
acceptable.why: A four-person seed team is paid to ship features, and these products already handle retries, signing, a customer-facing delivery log, endpoint disabling and replay. Comparing their price against the build cost is a legitimate decision.

acceptable.choice: Go for the delivery worker, as a deferred option
acceptable.why: Go would work technically and has low memory use per connection, but it only becomes worth it if measurements show Node can't keep up or costs too much, and even then it rests on the one developer who has written some Go.

acceptable.choice: A Postgres-backed queue (pg-boss, Graphile Worker) in place of BullMQ
acceptable.why: It's TypeScript-native and transactional with the outbox, which is attractive. It's acceptable only if the managed Postgres can absorb up to ~2,500 job writes per second at peak, so measure that first.

ruled_out.choice: Calling customer URLs inline in the Express request handler (or fire-and-forget promises inside the API process)
ruled_out.why: Breaks the hard requirement not to block the main API, and gives no durable retries: in-flight deliveries vanish on a deploy or crash.

ruled_out.choice: JVM stack (Java/Kotlin with Spring, Vert.x, etc.)
ruled_out.why: Nobody has run a JVM in production, it doesn't help with hiring TypeScript developers, and it brings new operational work for no benefit at this load.

ruled_out.choice: Rust or Elixir rewrite of the delivery path
ruled_out.why: Nobody on the team has these skills, it slows feature shipping, and it narrows hiring, all to solve a performance problem they don't have.

ruled_out.choice: Kafka / self-run event streaming platform as the delivery backbone
ruled_out.why: Far too much operational weight for four developers at 40–500 events per second, when Redis is already in the stack and enough.

ruled_out.choice: One serverless function invocation per delivery (Vercel Functions / AWS Lambda) as the main mechanism
ruled_out.why: You pay per invocation and per second spent waiting on 0.3–2 s (or timed-out) customer responses, at up to ~2,500 deliveries per second. The bill grows with traffic instead of slower than revenue, and retry scheduling still needs a queue anyway.

ruled_out.choice: Rewriting the whole API in Go as part of this project
ruled_out.why: Scope creep that stops feature work. Nothing about the webhook need justifies changing the main stack.

must_mention: Clear recommendation: write it in Node/TypeScript. This is I/O-bound, high-concurrency work, which is Node's strength, so a language change isn't justified.

Back-of-envelope sizing: peak ≈ 500 events/s × up to 5 endpoints ≈ 2,500 deliveries/s, and at ~1–2 s each that's roughly 2,500–5,000 requests in flight (more when calls time out). One event loop or a few small worker instances can hold that with a proper concurrency setting. Average load is about 100–200 deliveries/s.
Run it as a separate worker process or Fly app, scaled apart from the API, fed by a durable queue (BullMQ/Redis they already have). The API only records or enqueues the event.
Strict per-request timeouts (a few seconds), plus capped response-body reads, so timed-out URLs don't tie up connections or memory.
Retries with exponential backoff and jitter, a maximum attempt count or time window, a dead-letter queue, and automatically disabling endpoints that keep failing.
Per-endpoint isolation: concurrency limits and circuit breaking per customer URL, so one slow customer can't starve the rest (head-of-line blocking).
Delivery is at-least-once: send an event or delivery ID (idempotency key) and sign payloads with HMAC so customers can deduplicate and verify them.
Use a transactional outbox (or equivalent) so events aren't lost between the database commit and the enqueue, and turn on Redis persistence (AOF) if Redis holds the queue.
SSRF protection, because customers supply the URLs: block private/internal IP ranges (also after DNS resolution), restrict redirects and ports.
Name buying (Svix/Hookdeck) or self-hosting (Convoy) as a real alternative to building, given four developers and the priority on shipping features.
Revisit Go only on measured evidence, such as CPU per delivery, memory per instance, or Fly cost, not on reputation.
red_flags: Recommending Go (or Rust/JVM) mainly because 'Node is single-threaded' or 'Go is faster', when the bottleneck is network waiting, not CPU.
Ignoring the hiring and team-skills constraint, or putting a core service on the one developer who has 'written some Go'.
Making deliveries synchronous or in-process with the API, or using plain setTimeout/in-memory retries that disappear on deploys and restarts.
No timeouts on outbound calls, or relying on library defaults, which can hang for minutes or forever.
Treating one event's fan-out as a single job, so one failing endpoint triggers re-delivery to all the endpoints that already succeeded.
Claiming exactly-once delivery, or omitting idempotency keys and signatures.
Omitting SSRF risk from customer-supplied URLs.
Proposing Kafka, Kubernetes, or a service mesh for a four-person team at this volume.
A per-invocation serverless design without noting that cost scales with time spent waiting on slow customer endpoints.
Failing to compute even rough throughput and concurrency numbers, and asserting that Node will or won't scale without arithmetic.
unknowns: The actual peak concurrency and memory per in-flight request in Node on their Fly instance sizes. Load-test against a fake slow endpoint (300 ms–2 s, plus timeouts).
Whether their managed Redis plan (ops/s, memory, persistence/AOF, eviction policy) can sustain ~2,500 BullMQ jobs/s at peak plus delayed retry sets during a large customer outage.
Required delivery guarantees and SLAs: maximum delay, retry window (hours or days), ordering per customer or endpoint, and whether customers need replay.
Whether customers need a self-serve delivery log/UI and endpoint management. That changes the build-or-buy balance strongly toward Svix or Hookdeck.
Pricing of managed webhook services at their projected volume, compared with engineering time and Fly/Redis cost.
Retention and volume of delivery-attempt logs (millions of rows per day) and whether those belong in the main Postgres or need partitioning or TTL.
How growth is expected to scale: more events per customer or more endpoints per event, which decides when Node instances or Redis become the cost driver.
Payload sizes and whether any per-delivery CPU work (signing large payloads, transforms) is significant enough to matter.
